# STSX

> `.stsx` files are TSX plus raw-CSS `<style>` blocks, scoped by where you put them and compiled at build time to plain scoped CSS. `@lumiose/stsx` brings them to React, React Router and Solid through a Vite plugin; Lumiose apps use them natively.

These docs ship in `@lumiose/stsx` and match the installed version: `node_modules/@lumiose/stsx/docs`.
In Lumiose apps, `.stsx` is the component format: `node_modules/lumiose/docs/llms.txt`.

<!-- source: README.md -->

# STSX

> `.stsx` files are TSX plus raw-CSS `<style>` blocks, scoped by where you put them and compiled at build time to plain scoped CSS. `@lumiose/stsx` brings them to React, React Router and Solid through a Vite plugin; Lumiose apps use them natively.

```tsx
// Counter.stsx (React)
import { useState } from "react";
import { brand } from "./tokens.ts";

export function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <div className="counter">
      <style>
        .counter { display: flex; gap: 8px; }
        button { background: $brand.primary; color: white; }
      </style>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>count: {count}</button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

The block styles only `Counter`'s elements: its `button` rule reaches no other button in the app.
`$brand.primary` is a constant from `tokens.ts`, folded into the CSS at build time.

**What you get:**

- **Plain CSS** next to the markup, with nesting and modern syntax, and none of the class names
  you would otherwise have to invent.
- **No runtime.** Styles become a static stylesheet: extracted per route, minified and lowered
  by Vite like any CSS. Elements carry a small marker, an attribute or a class.
- **Scope by placement:** a block styles the file, a component, or one element's subtree,
  depending on where it sits.
- **Typed constants** shared between TypeScript and CSS, in values and in media queries.
- **Editor support:** TypeScript and CSS features, class-name completion and unused-selector
  warnings across the JSX and the blocks.

**Status:** new. `@lumiose/stsx` shares the version of the other Lumiose packages.
It has been tested with React 19, React Router 8 (framework mode, with server rendering) and Solid
1.9 on Vite 8. Other JSX frameworks whose Vite plugin compiles `.tsx` files should work, but are
untested.

## Pages

- [Installation](installation.md): the Vite plugin for React, React Router and Solid, and the
  tsconfig for type checking.
- [Styles](styles.md): placement and scope, global blocks, `$name` constants, `:global()` and
  `:deep()`, keyframes, dynamic values, specificity and class passthrough.
- [Options](options.md): `classAttribute` and `scopedStyles`.
- [React Router](react-router.md): components in `.stsx`, route modules in `.tsx`, and CSS per route.
- [Type checking and editors](type-checking.md): `stsx typegen`, `tsc` and the language server.

In a Lumiose app, `.stsx` is the component format and needs no plugin of its own: see
[Styles](https://itsjavi.com/lumiose/docs/concepts/styles/) in the Lumiose docs. These pages ship in
`@lumiose/stsx` (`node_modules/@lumiose/stsx/docs`), so they match the installed version.

<!-- source: installation.md -->

# Installation

> Add `@lumiose/stsx` to a Vite app before your framework's plugin, set `classAttribute` for the framework, and point the tsconfig at the shadow files so that `tsc` checks `.stsx` files.

```sh
pnpm add -D @lumiose/stsx
```

It needs Vite 8 and Node 24 or later. The plugin goes **before** the framework's plugin: it turns
each `.stsx` file into TSX for that plugin, and its `<style>` blocks into a stylesheet for Vite.

## React

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import stsx from "@lumiose/stsx";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [stsx({ classAttribute: "className" }), react()],
});
```

Fast Refresh works as with `.tsx` files. An edit inside a `<style>` block replaces the stylesheet
alone, without re-rendering.

## React Router

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { reactRouter } from "@react-router/dev/vite";
import stsx from "@lumiose/stsx";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [stsx({ classAttribute: "className" }), reactRouter()],
});
```

Route modules stay `.tsx` files and render components from `.stsx` files: see
[React Router](react-router.md).

## Solid

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import stsx from "@lumiose/stsx";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import solid from "vite-plugin-solid";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [stsx({ classAttribute: "class" }), solid()],
});
```

Solid compiles the scope markers into its static templates, so they cost nothing at runtime.
Elements that Solid creates later (in `<For>`, `<Show>`) carry them too.

## TypeScript

Add the shadow directory to `rootDirs` and `include`, so that `import "./Card.stsx"` type-checks:

```jsonc
// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "rootDirs": [".", ".lumiose/stsx"],
  },
  "include": ["src", ".lumiose/stsx"],
}
```

Add `.lumiose/` to `.gitignore`, and run `stsx typegen` before `tsc` in CI. Editors, other
directories and the details: [Type checking and editors](type-checking.md).

## Your first component

Rename a component file from `.tsx` to `.stsx` and add a `<style>` block next to the elements it
styles:

```tsx
// Card.stsx
export function Card({ title, children }: { title: string; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <article className="card">
      <style>
        .card { padding: 1rem; border-radius: 12px; background: #f4f4f5; }
        h2 { margin: 0 0 0.5rem; }
      </style>
      <h2>{title}</h2>
      {children}
    </article>
  );
}
```

Imports of `./Card.stsx` work like imports of `./Card.tsx`. The rules of the blocks: [Styles](styles.md).

<!-- source: styles.md -->

# Styles

> A `<style>` block holds plain CSS and styles what encloses it: the file at the top level, a component or one element's subtree inside JSX, or the whole app with `global`. Constants come from TypeScript with `$name`; `:global()` and `:deep()` cross the scope.

## Placement decides scope

| Placement                                       | Styles                                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Top level of the file (outside every component) | Every element of every component in the file                                    |
| Inside a component's JSX                        | The element that contains the block and everything inside it, in that component |
| `<style global>`, anywhere                      | The whole app, unscoped                                                         |

```tsx
export function Nav() {
  return (
    <nav>
      <style>
        a { color: inherit; }
      </style>
      <a href="/">Home</a>
    </nav>
  );
}

<style>
  nav { display: flex; gap: 1rem; }
</style>

<style global>
  body { margin: 0; }
</style>
```

A block inside JSX must be a static child of an element or fragment: not inside a condition, a
`.map()` or another `{…}` expression, and not the only thing a component returns. Use classes for
variations.

Every element in a scope carries the scope's marker, so dynamic classes and elements created
later (lists, conditions) match the scope's rules too. Elements rendered by **another component**
do not: reach them with `:deep()`, or with class passthrough (below).

## Plain CSS

Blocks are CSS, as in a `.css` file: nesting, `@media`, `@container`, `@supports`, `@layer`,
custom properties and modern syntax. Vite lowers it for your `build.cssTarget`, minifies it, and
extracts it into the stylesheet of the chunk or route that imports the component. Sass and other
`lang` attributes are not supported; import `.scss` files through Vite instead.

## Constants: `$name`

A `$name` reference in a value or in an `@media`, `@container` or `@supports` condition is
replaced at build time by a constant:

```tsx
import { BREAKPOINT, radius } from "./tokens.ts";

const accent = "#e11d48";

<style>
  .card { border-radius: $radius.lg; border-color: $accent; }
  @media (width < $BREAKPOINT) { .card { padding: 0; } }
</style>
```

- **Eligible.** Top-level `const` bindings of the file, `export const` imports from `.ts`,
  `.tsx` or `.stsx` modules, and local `const` bindings of the component (for a block in its JSX).
  Their values must be statically known: literals, template literals of constants, members of
  `as const` objects and arrays, and simple arithmetic.
- **Strings** go in as raw CSS text, **numbers** as they are: write `"8px"`, or
  `calc($gap * 1px)`.
- **Dot notation** for object members (`$brand.primary`); `$brand-primary` is an error, since
  JavaScript names cannot contain `-`.
- **Not replaced** in selectors, property names, strings, comments or `url()`. In selectors,
  `[href$=".pdf"]` keeps its CSS meaning.
- **Updates.** Editing `tokens.ts` in dev updates the CSS of every file that uses it.

CSS has no JavaScript expressions: blocks are static. For a value that changes at runtime, set a
custom property in the `style` prop and read it with `var()`:

```tsx
<div className="bar" style={{ "--progress": `${percent}%` }}>
  <style>
    .bar { width: var(--progress); }
  </style>
</div>
```

## Escapes: `:global()` and `:deep()`

- **`:global(sel)`** leaves `sel` unscoped: `.menu :global(.icon)` styles any `.icon` inside the
  menu, and `:global(body.dark) .menu` reads a class on `<body>`.
- **`:deep(sel)`** scopes only what is on its left: `.card :deep(a)` styles links that a child
  component renders inside `.card`.

## Keyframes

`@keyframes` names are scoped per block's scope, and `animation` and `animation-name` references
to them are rewritten, so two components can each define `@keyframes spin` without a clash.

## Specificity

By default a scoped selector gets one extra attribute or class, a (0,1,0) bump: `.note` becomes
`.note[data-lum-a1b2c3d4]`. A component's rules then win over global rules of the same
specificity. With `scopedStyles: { specificity: "zero" }` the marker goes inside `:where()` and
adds nothing, so a global or utility class written later wins ([Options](options.md)).

## Class passthrough

With `scopedStyles: { strategy: "class" }`, the scope travels with the class you pass to a
component:

```tsx
// Parent.stsx
import { Button } from "./Button.tsx";

export function Toolbar() {
  return (
    <div>
      <style>
        .cta { font-weight: bold; }
      </style>
      <Button className="cta">Save</Button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

The parent's scope classes are appended to `className`. A `Button` that puts `props.className` on
its element, as most components do, receives them, and `.cta` styles it. With the default
attribute strategy, use `:deep()` instead.

## Diagnostics

The plugin reports problems in the dev overlay and the build output, with a code frame:

- **`LUM3005`, unused selector.** A selector that matches no element of its scope (it reads
  `classAttribute`).
- **`LUM3008`, unresolvable constant.** A `$name` that is not a constant.
- **`LUM3009`, hyphenated reference.** `$brand-primary`.
- **`LUM3010` and `LUM3011`, misplaced block.** A block in a condition, or one that is a
  component's only output.
- **`LUM3014` to `LUM3020`.** CSS syntax and value problems.

Each code has a page in the [Lumiose error reference](https://itsjavi.com/lumiose/docs/errors/).

<!-- source: options.md -->

# Options

> `stsx({ classAttribute, scopedStyles })`: the JSX attribute that holds classes (required), and how scoped elements are marked and matched: attribute or class, default or zero specificity, and the marker's namespace.

```ts
stsx({
  classAttribute: "className", // required: "className" or "class"
  scopedStyles: {
    strategy: "attribute", // or "class"
    specificity: "default", // or "zero"
    namespace: "lum",
  },
});
```

Invalid options stop Vite when the config loads, with the option and the expected values.

## `classAttribute`

The attribute that holds class names in your JSX: `"className"` for React and Preact, `"class"`
for Solid. The unused-selector check (`LUM3005`) reads it. With the class strategy, the scope
classes are merged into it, and class passthrough appends the parent's scope to the one passed to
a component.

## `scopedStyles`

| `strategy`            | `specificity`       | Element                     | `.note` becomes                    |
| --------------------- | ------------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `attribute` (default) | `default` (default) | `data-lum-a1b2c3d4`         | `.note[data-lum-a1b2c3d4]`         |
| `attribute`           | `zero`              | `data-lum-a1b2c3d4`         | `.note:where([data-lum-a1b2c3d4])` |
| `class`               | `default`           | `class="note lum-a1b2c3d4"` | `.note.lum-a1b2c3d4`               |
| `class`               | `zero`              | `class="note lum-a1b2c3d4"` | `.note:where(.lum-a1b2c3d4)`       |

- **`strategy: "attribute"`** adds empty `data-<namespace>-<hash>` attributes and leaves your
  class names alone.
- **`strategy: "class"`** merges `<namespace>-<hash>` classes into `classAttribute`: appended to
  a string, combined with a computed value, added to an element without one. It also enables
  class passthrough to child components ([Styles](styles.md#class-passthrough)). Choose it when
  something strips or rejects `data-*` attributes, or for passthrough.
- **`specificity: "zero"`** wraps the marker in `:where()`: scoped rules then tie with global rules
  of the same specificity, and source order decides. Choose it when global styles or utility
  classes should override component styles without `!important`. Every evergreen browser
  supports `:where()`.
- **`namespace`** starts with a lowercase letter and holds lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.
  Change it to avoid clashes with another library's markers.

The hash is stable: it comes from the file's path relative to the project root (and the
component's name), so builds on different machines produce the same markers. A `.stsx` file in a
linked workspace package outside the root is named relative to its package.

<!-- source: react-router.md -->

# React Router

> In React Router's framework mode, components can be `.stsx` files: their CSS is linked per route in server-rendered HTML, in dev and production. Route modules stay `.tsx` files that render those components.

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { reactRouter } from "@react-router/dev/vite";
import stsx from "@lumiose/stsx";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [stsx({ classAttribute: "className" }), reactRouter()],
});
```

## Route modules are `.tsx`

React Router finds a route module by the file path in `routes.ts`, and strips its server-only
exports (`loader`, `action`) from the client build. It does that only for files it compiles
itself, so a route module cannot be a `.stsx` file: the plugin stops the build with an error that
says so. Keep the route in `.tsx`, and put the markup and its styles in a `.stsx` component:

```tsx
// app/routes/about.tsx
import { AboutCard } from "../components/AboutCard.stsx";
import type { Route } from "./+types/about";

export function loader() {
  return { message: "Hello from the loader" };
}

export default function About({ loaderData }: Route.ComponentProps) {
  return <AboutCard message={loaderData.message} />;
}
```

```tsx
// app/components/AboutCard.stsx
export function AboutCard({ message }: { message: string }) {
  return (
    <section className="about">
      <h1>About</h1>
      <p className="message">{message}</p>
    </section>
  );
}

<style>
  .about { padding: 20px; border-radius: 14px; background: #d1fae5; }
  .message { font-style: italic; }
</style>
```

`root.tsx` can render `.stsx` components too: a layout shell, a navigation bar.

## CSS per route

- **Production.** Each route's stylesheet holds the CSS of the `.stsx` components it imports.
  React Router links it in the route's server-rendered `<head>`, and client navigations load it
  before the route renders.
- **Dev.** React Router's critical CSS includes the `.stsx` styles, so pages do not flash
  unstyled. An edit inside a `<style>` block hot-replaces the stylesheet alone, once per save.
- **Styling a `NavLink` or `Link`.** It renders its `<a>` in your component's markup, but as
  another component's element: reach it with `:deep()`, as in `nav :deep(a.active)`, or use the
  class strategy so the scope travels with its `className`.

## Types

React Router's route types and the `.stsx` shadows share `rootDirs`:

```jsonc
// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "rootDirs": [".", "./.react-router/types", ".lumiose/stsx"],
  },
  "include": ["app", ".react-router/types", ".lumiose/stsx"],
}
```

```sh
stsx typegen && react-router typegen && tsc
```

<!-- source: type-checking.md -->

# Type checking and editors

> TypeScript checks `.stsx` files through shadow TSX files that `stsx typegen` and the Vite plugin write to `.lumiose/stsx`. The Lumiose language server and VS Code extension give `.stsx` files TypeScript and CSS features in any project.

## Shadows

TypeScript does not know `.stsx`. For each `.stsx` file, a TSX copy (the "shadow") is written to
`.lumiose/stsx/<the file's path>.stsx.tsx`. Its style blocks are blanked out and every other
character keeps its position, so the shadow type-checks like the component and every line and
column matches the `.stsx` file. With `rootDirs`, `import "./Card.stsx"` resolves to the shadow:

```jsonc
// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "rootDirs": [".", ".lumiose/stsx"],
  },
  "include": ["src", ".lumiose/stsx"],
}
```

- **Who writes them.** The Vite plugin writes every shadow when the dev server or a build starts,
  and rewrites a file's shadow when you edit it. `stsx typegen` writes them all and removes those
  of deleted files, for CI and other scripts.
- **The tsconfig hint.** Without the `rootDirs` entry, `stsx typegen` prints the line to add.
- **Version control.** Add `.lumiose/` to `.gitignore`: the shadows are generated.
- **Another directory.** Name it `stsx` in `rootDirs`, as in `[".", ".types/stsx"]`. The plugin and
  `stsx typegen` use it; the language server reads `.lumiose/stsx` only.

```sh
stsx typegen && tsc
```

`tsc` names the shadow in its errors (`.lumiose/stsx/src/Card.stsx.tsx(12,7)`), at the line and
column of the `.stsx` file.

## Constants in CSS

`$name` references in style blocks become expressions in the shadow, so TypeScript checks them
too: a missing export or member (`$brand.nope`) is a type error at the reference, and go to
definition and rename work on it.

## Editors

The Lumiose VS Code extension handles `.stsx` files in any project; other editors run
`@lumiose/language-server`, which it bundles. In a project that depends on `@lumiose/stsx` and
not on `lumiose`, the server runs in **stsx mode**:

- **TypeScript:** completion, hover, go to definition, references, rename and type errors,
  through the shadows;
- **CSS** in style blocks: completion, hover, colors and syntax errors;
- **Class names** between the JSX (`class`, `className`, Solid's `classList`) and the blocks:
  completion, go to definition, rename and unused-selector warnings;
- **None of Lumiose's own checks:** no reactivity or island diagnostics and no
  execution-contract hovers, since your framework's JSX is not Lumiose's.

GitHub highlights `.stsx` as TSX with a line in `.gitattributes`:

```text
*.stsx linguist-language=TSX
```
